content: Multi-strategic community-wide interventions aimed at increasing physical activity are becoming more popular, but their effectiveness in achieving population-level improvements remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of such interventions on physical activity levels across populations. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and others, as well as websites of relevant organizations such as the CDC and NICE. The search was updated to January 16, 2014, and included studies regardless of language or publication status. Eligible studies included cluster randomized controlled trials, randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental designs with control populations, interrupted time-series studies, and prospective controlled cohort studies. Only studies with a minimum follow-up of six months from the start of the intervention were included. Interventions had to involve at least two broad strategies targeting physical activity at the population level. Studies that randomized individuals within the same community were excluded. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by at least two reviewers. The primary outcomes were categorized as either dichotomous (e.g., percentage of individuals physically active, percentage physically active during leisure time, percentage physically inactive) or continuous (e.g., time spent in leisure-time physical activity, walking, or energy expenditure measured in metabolic equivalents or METs). For dichotomous outcomes, unadjusted and adjusted risk differences and relative risks were calculated. For continuous outcomes, percentage changes from baseline were analyzed. A total of 33 studies involving 267 communities (populations ranging from 500 to 1.9 million) were included in the review. Of these, 25 studies were conducted in high-income countries, while eight were conducted in low-income countries. The interventions varied in the number and intensity of strategies employed, with most including partnerships with local governments or non-governmental organizations (29 studies). However, none of the studies reported results based on socio-economic disadvantage or other equity markers. Among the studies conducted in high-income countries, 14 targeted deprived or low socio-economic communities. The risk of bias was a significant concern in the included studies. Nineteen studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, 10 had unclear risk, and only four were considered to have a low risk of bias. Selection bias was particularly problematic, with only five studies using randomization to allocate communities. Four studies were deemed to have a low risk of selection bias, while 19 had unclear risk. Detection bias was also an issue, with 12 studies at high risk, 13 at unclear risk, and four at low risk. The better-designed studies generally showed no improvement in physical activity at the population level. Four newly included studies, judged to have a low risk of bias, used randomization to allocate interventions to communities. These studies, conducted in Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States, employed either cluster randomized or stepped wedge designs. The measurement of physical activity outcomes was more robust in these studies compared to earlier ones. One study used accelerometers to obtain objective, population-representative data, while the other three relied on validated self-reported measures. The study using accelerometry, conducted in low-income, high-crime communities in the United States, focused on social marketing, partnerships with police, and environmental improvements. However, no change in the average daily minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity over seven days was observed during the two-year intervention period. Some program-level effects were noted, such as increased walking in the intervention community, but these effects were not evident at the whole-community level. Similarly, two studies conducted in the United Kingdom (one in rural villages and the other in urban London) found no improvement in mean energy expenditure per person per week, measured one to four years from baseline. None of the three low-risk studies reporting dichotomous physical activity outcomes found improvements associated with the interventions. Overall, the included studies did not demonstrate consistent benefits in physical activity levels from community-wide interventions. However, interventions conducted in China appeared to show the greatest potential for success, with high participation rates reported. Reporting bias was evident, as two studies failed to report physical activity outcomes at follow-up. No adverse events were reported in any of the studies. Data on the cost and sustainability of the interventions were limited and varied. In conclusion, despite the large number of studies conducted, the evidence does not support the hypothesis that multi-component community-wide interventions effectively increase physical activity at the population level. Methodological issues and inconsistencies in the findings further complicate the interpretation of results. While some interventions with environmental components observed increased walking, these effects were not consistently observed across studies.
